title: Carving a deep-bowl spoon: hook-knife technique
subtitle: How to carve a properly deep bowl using a hook knife
excerpt: Most beginners undercarve the bowl and end up with a spoon that holds only a few drops. This technique guide covers the hook-knife arc, the catch-and-correct sequence when the blade stalls, and the wall-thickness check that tells you when to stop.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the hook-knife method in treen-making.

glossaryTerms.definition: A curved-bladed knife for hollowing the bowl of a spoon or kuksa. Right- and left-handed variants are not interchangeable.
Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. The ideal state for hook-knife work, the wood offers far less resistance than seasoned timber.
A leather strap charged with abrasive compound, used to maintain a sharp edge between honings.

content.text: The hook-knife hollow is the step that separates a functional spoon from a decorative one. A correctly hollowed bowl holds soup; an undercarved bowl does not. The technique itself is simple, a drawing arc with the wrist rather than a push from the arm, but beginners consistently undercarve because the wood feels like it's resisting before the bowl is anywhere near deep enough. This guide covers the full arc sequence, the stalling fix, and the light test that shows when the walls are ready to stop.
When to use this technique

Any spoon or kuksa project that needs a deep, cleanly hollowed bowl. A jam spoon needs 3, 5 mm depth; an eating spoon or soup spoon needs 8, 12 mm at the centre; a kuksa needs 20 mm or more. The hook knife is the only hand tool that can reach the centre of a bowl deeper than about 3 mm without damage to the rim.
What you need
A
hook knife

sized to the bowl: a small hook for jam spoons and tea spoons, a medium hook for eating and serving spoons. The edge must be sharp: stropped and then honed on a slipstone if it has been used for more than one session. A dull hook knife is the most common cause of undercarved bowls. The spoon blank should still be in
green wood
state, dried blanks resist the hook knife considerably more.
The technique: step by step
1. Grip and body position

Hold the spoon blank with your non-dominant hand, flat face up, bowl end pointing toward your knife hand. Your non-dominant thumb rests at the base of the bowl, fingers wrapped underneath the blank. The
strop
should be within reach, you will use it every fifteen minutes.
2. The drawing arc

Place the hook knife at the far rim of the bowl, hook pointing into the bowl at about 30 degrees to the surface. Draw the knife toward you in a curving arc, ending when the blade exits the near rim. The power comes from the wrist and forearm; the shoulder does not move. Each arc should lift a thin, clean shaving, about the thickness of a playing card. If you are getting thick chunks, the hook is too steep into the wood; flatten the entry angle slightly.
3. Working around the bowl

After each arc, rotate the blank a few degrees so the next cut overlaps the previous one by about half. Work around the entire rim of the bowl before going deeper. This even first pass sets the bowl shape; carving deeply on one side first gives an uneven bowl.
4. Going deeper

After a full circuit of the bowl, repeat from the rim again, this time starting the arc slightly lower on the bowl wall. Work inward in concentric passes. The centre of the bowl is always the last area to deepen, this keeps the wall thickness even. If the centre resists more than the sides, the grain is running in a different direction at the centre (common in off-centre blanks cut near the pith). Rotate the blank 180 degrees and cut from the other side of the bowl.
5. When the blade stalls

If the hook knife stops cutting and drags instead of peeling, there are three causes: edge dull (strop immediately), cutting against the grain (rotate the blank and cut from the other side), or entry angle too steep (flatten to 20, 25 degrees). Never force a stalled hook knife, the blade can skip out of the bowl and into your hand.
What a correctly carved bowl looks like

Hold the spoon up to a window or a lamp so the light shines through the bowl from the back. A well-carved bowl shows an even, slightly translucent glow across the whole bowl face, the wall is uniformly thin (3, 5 mm for a spoon). Dark spots mean thick patches; bright spots mean thin patches that risk breaking. The bowl surface, viewed at a low angle, should show a clean scalloped pattern of overlapping cuts with no ridges between them.
Common mistakes
Undercarving: stopping when the bowl looks deep enough from above, rather than checking the wall thickness from behind. The front view is misleading. Use the light test.

Chasing the grain at the rim: the rim is where the grain changes direction on most spoon blanks. If the rim is tearing rather than cutting, switch to a push-cut with the sloyd knife for that area and use the hook knife only for the deeper centre.

Buying the wrong hook-knife hand: hook knives are handed. A right-hand hook in a left hand (or vice versa) cannot make the correct drawing arc without rotating the wrist to an unsafe angle. Check the hook direction when buying.
